title: Are AI Investing Apps in India Actually Worth Using?

content:
For most salaried investors, yes, an AI investing app is worth using. But only if it routes you to direct mutual fund plans. Most apps in India don't, and whether your app holds a SEBI Investment Adviser registration or operates as a fund distributor is the one thing worth checking first.

Monthly SIP contributions hit a record Rs 32,490 crore in September 2026, per AMFI data. More money is flowing into these apps than ever. This post is for information only and is not financial advice.

Key Takeaways

  • Most Indian AI investing apps are SEBI-registered fund distributors, not Investment Advisers. They earn commissions and typically put you in regular plans.
  • Direct mutual fund plans cost 0.5 to 1.5 percentage points less per year than the regular plan of the same fund.
  • Fewer than 1,000 SEBI-registered RIAs serve India's 20 crore-plus active investors, so genuine fee-only advice is scarce.
  • For straightforward SIPs with a corpus under Rs 50 lakh, a free direct-plan platform is usually the better call.
  • Complex finances like NRI status, business income, or ESOPs justify a SEBI-registered fee-only RIA.

What "AI Advisor" Usually Means in India

SEBI does not license a separate robo-advisor category. Any platform giving personalized investment advice needs an Investment Adviser (IA) registration. Most Indian consumer apps register as Mutual Fund Distributors instead, which means they earn a commission from fund houses and typically recommend regular plans, not direct ones.

An MFD earns a trail commission from the Asset Management Company for as long as your money stays in a regular plan. This cost isn't visible as a line item. You pay a higher expense ratio: typically 0.7 to 1.5 percent per year more than the direct plan of the same fund. That gap is entirely seperate from whatever the AI chat interface looks like on the front end.

A SEBI-registered IA charges you directly. They earn nothing from fund houses, so they can freely recommend direct plans. Scripbox holds an IA registration. Groww, INDmoney and ET Money are execution platforms that let you buy direct mutual funds at no charge, but they don't provide personalized advice in the registered IA sense.

What Can These Apps Actually Do For You?

They'll build a goal-based portfolio from your income and risk tolerance. They'll send rebalancing alerts when your allocation drifts. The algorithm is often a better starting point than guessing which funds to pick yourself. But they can't execute automatically. SEBI requires your explicit approval for every transaction, so automated investing in India means automated recommendations, not automated action.

They also won't catch nuances in complex situations: whether a debt fund is more tax-efficient than an FD for your specific tax bracket, how your employer's ESOP allocation affects your actual equity exposure, or whether you're overconcentrated across PF, NPS and direct equity. Those calls need a conversation, not an alert.

Also worth knowing: Indian apps currently can't do automatic tax-loss harvesting or automatic rebalancing the way some US platforms do. What you recieve is a recommendation, not a completed trade.

Is Paying For an AI Investing App Worth It?

If you're begining to invest seriously and your finances are straightforward, the honest answer is usually no. This holds for most portfolios under Rs 50 lakh with a single income source. Pick a free platform that defaults to direct plans and you've solved the main problem. Groww, INDmoney and ET Money all offer direct mutual fund investing at no charge.

Say you're putting Rs 30,000 a month into a regular plan with a 1.8 percent expense ratio instead of the same fund's direct plan at 0.5 percent. Over 15 years at 12 percent nominal returns, the difference in net corpus is roughly Rs 6 to 8 lakh. That's real money that disappears into the distributor's commission without you seeing it as a fee.

The math shifts above Rs 50 lakh or when your finances get complicated. A SEBI-registered RIA can charge up to roughly Rs 1.5 lakh a year, but on a large corpus with complex tax needs they typically earn it back. Verify their SEBI registration at sebi.gov.in before engaging anyone.

One honest caveat on the free apps: free means execution, not advice. Groww and INDmoney don't review whether your portfolio still matches your goals as your life changes. That's the gap a paid service fills, and for large portfolios, it's a real gap worth paying for.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are AI investing apps in India regulated by SEBI?

Yes, but "AI advisor" isn't a regulated term. Any platform giving personalized investment advice must hold a SEBI Investment Adviser registration. Many Indian apps are registered as Mutual Fund Distributors instead, a different category with different conflict-of-interest rules. Always check a platform's SEBI registration type before committing money.

What is the difference between a direct and a regular mutual fund plan?

A direct plan eliminates the distributor's trail commission, so the fund's annual expense ratio is lower by roughly 0.5 to 1.5 percent. The underlying portfolio is identical. Over a 10 to 15 year horizon, this cost difference compounds into a meaningful amount. SEBI-registered advisers must recommend direct plans; distributor platforms often default to regular.

Can an AI investing app place trades automatically in India?

No. SEBI requires investor approval for every transaction. Indian apps can recommend when to buy or rebalance your portfolio, but every action requires your explicit confirmation. Fully automated execution, the kind available on some US platforms, is not legally permitted in India under current SEBI regulations.

Is Scripbox a SEBI-registered Investment Adviser?

Scripbox holds a SEBI Investment Adviser registration, which allows it to give personalized advice and charge you directly rather than earning commissions from fund houses. Its advisory fee is roughly 0.5 percent of AUM per year. Verify current registration status at sebi.gov.in before committing funds, since registrations can change.

When should I use a fee-only RIA instead of an app?

When your portfolio exceeds Rs 50 lakh, or when your finances include NRI status, business income, ESOPs, or estate planning. A SEBI-registered RIA earns nothing from fund houses, owes you unbiased advice, and typically earns back their fee through better tax efficiency and allocation at larger corpus sizes.

The Short Version

Most Indian AI investing apps earn from your expense ratio, not a subscription. For simple SIPs, use a free platform that defaults to direct plans. For complex or large portfolios, a SEBI-registered fee-only RIA earns their fee. The AI label on an app doesn't tell you which category it falls into. Check the SEBI registration first.
